summary: This excerpt from Marx's Wage-Labour and Capital-style lecture (Value, Price and Profit) argues that the exchange value of a commodity is determined by the socially necessary labour crystallized in it, not by wages or market fluctuations. It then distinguishes labour from labour power, explains how the value of labour power is set by the cost of its necessaries, and shows how surplus value arises when a worker's labour power is used beyond the time needed to reproduce its value. The note closes by showing how wage labour disguises unpaid labour as paid labour, contrasted with slave and serf labour.
one_line: Marx's lecture explaining that commodity value rests on socially necessary labour, and how surplus value arises from the sale of labouring power.
key_facts: The value of a commodity is determined by the quantity of socially necessary labour crystallized in it, measured by time of labour.
Benjamin Franklin used the example of equal labour in one quarter of wheat and one ounce of gold in his 1721 Essay A Modest Enquiry into the Nature and Necessity of a Paper Currency.
The values of commodities are directly as the times of labour employed in their production, and inversely as the productive powers of the labour employed.
Adam Smith called the monetary expression of value the natural price, and the French physiocrats called it prix necessaire.
Adam Smith wrote that the natural price is the central price to which the prices of commodities are continually gravitating.
Mr. Tooke's History of Prices is cited as an example of analyzing market price movements over longer periods.
When the power-loom competed with the hand-loom in England, only half the former time of labour was needed to convert a given amount of yarn into a yard of cloth.
Thomas Hobbes, in his Leviathan, said the value or worth of a man is his price, that is, as much as would be given for the use of his power.
The value of labouring power is determined by the value of the necessaries required to produce, develop, maintain, and perpetuate the labouring power.
In the example, six hours of average labour is realized in daily necessaries worth 3s., so 3s. is the daily value of the spinner's labouring power.
If the spinner works twelve hours, he adds six shillings of value to the cotton, while the capitalist pays only three shillings in wages.
The rate of surplus value depends on the ratio in which the working day is prolonged beyond the time needed to reproduce the value of labouring power.
The author says the cry for equality of wages is an inane wish never to be fulfilled, since different labouring powers have different values.
Wage labour makes even unpaid labour appear to be paid labour, whereas with the slave even paid labour appears unpaid.
